analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "We'll hear arguments next in number 71, 827, Hughes Tool Company against Transworld Airlines, and 830, Transworld Airlines against Hughes Tool. Mr. Wright, the papers before me right at the moment do not indicate whether the parties made a request for additional time. Neither party has made such a request, Your Honor. Very well. We have not. No, sir. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the Court, in the 30 minutes that we have, it is obvious that neither I nor Mr. Tenney are going to be able to discuss comprehensively all of the 11 issues on which the Court granted certiorari on the petition and the cross-petition, but we are going to have to let our briefs speak for us on many of those issues. Indeed, I consider my time to be somewhat less than 30 minutes because I'm quite determined to close my initial submission while there is still some time remaining for rebuttal. And so in this time that I have, I want to go immediately to what seems to me the central overriding issue in this case, that I represent a corporation that has been ordered to pay the largest money judgment ever entered under the antitrust laws in a case that has nothing whatever to do with the antitrust laws. Whatever else my client may have done, my client did not violate the antitrust laws, and even with all the benefits that my friends from TWA have by virtue of the default judgment, it is impossible to make out a violation of the antitrust laws. There are three separate reasons, separate and independent, why this is not really an antitrust case. In the first place, the conduct, the facts alleged in the complaint, the facts proven by TWA at the damage hearing, show conduct on the part of defendants that as a matter of law cannot be held to violate the Sherman or Clayton Acts. Second, if there had been any antitrust violations in this case, we would have a complete defense of immunity under Section 414 of the Federal Aviation Act, because everything that my client has shown to have done in this case was done in the exercise, the normal exercise, of control of TWA approved by the Civil Aeronautics Board. Third, even if there had been antitrust violations and they were not immunized, the damages that have been awarded to TWA bear no relation to the supposed antitrust violations. The damages are that certain aircraft, jet aircraft, were ordered by TULCO, the parent company, for its carrier subsidiary, TWA, a few weeks later than they should have been. The TULCO subsequently decided that TWA should have only 47 first-generation jets and cut back the initial order that had been for 63 first-generation jets. But TULCO leased some of these aircraft to TWA for a period pending permanent financing and that leasing is a more expensive way of acquiring aircraft than is purchasing them outright. And finally, there is a small item that alleges that TULCO disrupted Convair's production and so some other planes came a little later than they should have. Now, what happened in this case, in my submission, is this. It was obvious that at the end of the 1950s, when the air carriers were converting to jet aircraft, it was obvious that neither TWA nor the parent company, TULCO, would be able, with its own resources, to pay the many millions of dollars required to acquire jets. It was going to be necessary to finance the acquisition of these aircraft by going to lending institutions. The eastern lending institutions, the banks and the insurance companies, would not make that financing available until TULCO, the owner of 78 percent of TWA, agreed to put its stock into a voting trust. The institutions controlled the voting trust. They put in a new board of directors for TWA. They put in new management for TWA. And the first thing that the new management does is to bring the present action against the owners and those who have formerly controlled the operation of TWA. They chose to cast the case in antitrust terms. This gives them federal jurisdiction that they would not otherwise have had. It gives them, if they are successful, treble damages. But I think that it's on the record that the principal motive for bringing a case on an antitrust theory was that they were primarily interested in forcing TULCO to divest itself of its interest in TWA. And they believed that the vestiture was a remedy that they might get in an antitrust case, though they could not get it, in a corporate mismanagement action. How does their motive bear on the issues here, Mr. Rick? It bears in this way. They got ultimately what they wanted. TULCO is out. And it seems to me not unjust, Justice Rehnquist, for us now to hold them strictly to their antitrust claim, not to feel sorry that, well, perhaps TWA simply picked its wrong theory, and it's like the plaintiff in Dio Guardi v. Durning with his home-drawn complaint, and we ought to strain hard to save him. I think that they followed a course with their eyes wide open, and that now they have to live or die with whether or not the theory they chose was a legally viable one. We think that demonstrably it is not. I was interested in a document TWA filed last week, labeled Memorandum in Response to Petitioner's Reply Brief, for two reasons. First, in our reply brief, our principal thrust had been that after all the hundreds of pages the TWA has written in briefs that the court below wrote, we still have not been told, A, in what respect did TULCO and the other defendants violate the antitrust laws? B, what is the immunity that you get when the CAB approves acquisition under Section 408? Of course, I'm sure, Mr. Wright, before we're through, someone's going to suggest that perhaps that should have been threshed out at an earlier date before a default occurred. Mr. Chief Justice, I think that is just what we had hoped would be threshed out at a much earlier stage by following the course that we did, choosing not to defend on the facts, and saying we are willing to stand or fall on the legal position we have in this case. Now, the event since February 8, 1963, had been convoluted. Obviously, it did not produce the expeditious determination of the case that we thought that it would. But it seems to me that it would have been irresponsible for my clients to have persisted in litigating the facts in a case of this sort that would take so much time for the federal court when, in our view, the facts make no difference whatever. Yes, Mr. Tenney, we're willing to concede all that you want to say about our motive and intent, because we simply do not think that the bad motives that we may have had hidden are enough to make an antitrust violation out of conduct that does not violate the antitrust laws. And we thought that we could get that legal issue before the court. We expected to prevail on it very quickly. We have not prevailed quickly. We hope to prevail now, nine years later. But it interested me that in the memorandum, in response to the reply brief, that TWA still does not undertake to answer either of these questions. We still don't know. They say again, as they said in their principal submission, that we have not disproven the fact that we could not have violated the antitrust laws in some way. We say, how do we violate the antitrust laws? That we give you the benefit of admitting all of your factual allegations, and I include ultimate fact as well as evidentiary fact, and constrain them as liberally as possible in the light of the damage hearing. But still, it ought to be possible then to look at the record and spell out some coherent theory on which my defendants, my clients, can be held to have violated the antitrust laws. I think that cannot be done. The second thing that interested me in their memorandum is that they pick up the example that we posed in both of our earlier submissions about an acquisition of TWA by Lockheed. This time, my friends call it a reductia ad absurdum. And on the difference between the two sides on that example, I am quite willing to stand or fall, because I think that that is a clear and decisive illustration of the difference between our legal positions on the effect of CAV immunity, and with a change in the facts, it also becomes a very interesting illustration of the difference between us on the supposed antitrust violations. The example, your honors will recall, is imagine that in 1946, when TWA was on the verge of bankruptcy, that nobody wanted to acquire the company. The carrier was about to fail, except Lockheed. And suppose that Lockheed said, okay, we'll buy control, CAB, if you'll approve it. The CAB knows that to allow a major manufacturer of airplanes to acquire a carrier means that Lockheed will be the exclusive supplier for TWA. It recognizes that a vertical integration of this kind is going to reduce competition. But the CAB says, we're required to look not just to antitrust, we're required to look at the public interest, and we think that the continued operation and solvency of TWA is so much in the public interest that it justifies this incidental restraint on competition. And so we, the CAB, will approve the acquisition of control, and just to make sure that Lockheed doesn't overstep, we'll put a condition on it that Lockheed can't sell any planes to TWA without our CAB approval. That way we'll be sure they don't force unnecessary planes on TWA. In the view of my friends, Lockheed, under those circumstances, would be liable to an antitrust action because it did exactly what the CAB knew that it was going to do, said that it could do, because the CAB found that other things outweighed the effect on competition. We think, in that illustration, that the CAB approval would be a complete grant of immunity. TWA says to argue that would immunize the antitrust violations there as a reductio absurdum. I think that the lines there are quite clearly drawn. But I would also vary the facts of my Lockheed illustration. Let us suppose that Lockheed is a super-responsible corporate parent, and so it says to TWA, having acquired control with CAB approval, Let us suppose it's what kind of a corporate? Super-responsible. Super-responsible. Yes. It says, much as we would love to sell you Lockheed planes, TWA, if you tell us you want Boeings and Convairs, fine. We want you to have exactly the planes that you want to have. And TWA says, well, we really would like to have some Boeings and Convairs. And so Lockheed, using its money, because TWA doesn't have any, goes down the street to Boeing and Convair and says, sell us some planes. And these planes, Lockheed in turn, then either leases or when it gets financing, it sells to TWA. Now, this would be much more of an antitrust violation, and my friends, there is, than anything that we have in our case, where TULCO is, in fact, not a manufacturer of planes, as Lockheed, of course, is. And yet, my friends would still be able to say, well, but Lockheed forced TWA to boycott Boeing and Convair, even though TWA ends up getting Boeing and Convair planes, because Lockheed insisted you can only buy planes from us, and we're going to be the conduit. That's what all the talk in this case about boycotts, tying arrangements, exclusive dealings are, that TULCO was the conduit. It acquired planes from Boeing and Convair and made them available to its subsidiary, TWA. This, we think, with or without CAB approval, simply is not a violation of the antitrust laws, that for a parent to acquire goods for its subsidiary, even for a parent to decide what goods its subsidiary is going to have, how many of them is going to have. We have here no restraint on competition of the sort to which the antitrust laws are directed. And if the parent goes to the trouble of making the subsidiary promise not to get planes from any source except through the parent, you say that's just beside the point. It's just a... That's just expressing what would happen anyway, because it is in control. Is that why you say... That is exactly my submission, Justice White. So that a parent in these circumstances, especially if approved by the CAB, can make the sub-promise not to buy planes anyplace else? Without any... No problem under the antitrust law. Well, since the subsidiary can't buy planes in any instance without the consent of its parent, it hardly matters whether you coerce this terrible-sounding promise out of the subsidiary. Well, that... Maybe ultimately that's right, but if you have a... A board of directors runs the company, and just what if it happens to vote to buy some planes somewhere else? I suppose it could, unless it was under some contractual promise to the parent. I suppose it could, but I... You're just assuming that, obviously, and maybe that's quite right that the parent will have a control of the board. If I control 78% of a corporation, I'd be surprised if this board of directors voted contrary to my wishes. Well, yes, but the board of directors might say, well, we have obligations as directors, too. Yes. To this corporate entity. Yes. And if we coerce our elected directors who control the board to do something that is wrong, something that is not in the interest of the corporation, then I say that, of course, a corporate mismanagement action will lie. But not an antitrust. Not an antitrust action, yes. That's the whole point of our case here. I, of course, do not concede for a moment, as a matter of fact, as differentiated from what my legal position has to be here, I don't concede that there was any mismanagement on the part of Tulka, but legally I'm in the posture that I have to admit it. But there was the promise not to buy planes anywhere else. By the default, that stands admitted, yes. Given 100% ownership on the part of the parent of the subsidiary, Mr. Wright, did you say nonetheless that the subsidiary could not be a plaintiff and bring a state of claim for relief against the parent in the antitrust law? The subsidiary certainly could bring an antitrust action, or if it were not 100% owned, a minority stockholder could bring a derivative action on its behalf, challenging the acquisition of control by the parent. But so far as the cases that either side has been able to produce go, that is the extent of it. And my friends have not been able to cite a case in which the challenge is solely to antitrust violations that the parent is alleged to have committed to the harm of the subsidiary after a lawful acquisition. I must say, Mr. Justice Rehnquist, I've been reflecting on that question in the last few days, trying to see if I could hypothesize a case in which there might be such a case. I hesitate to say that it could not ever happen, but I've been unable to think of an example in which the subsidiary would have an antitrust claim against the parent for activity after acquisition. I can well imagine, of course, and I want to be sure that this distinction is understood, I can well imagine cases in which third parties might have claims that because of the way the parent exercises control of the subsidiary... It's a keeper steward in the several cases. Sure, we have lots of cases of that kind, but that isn't our case here. We don't have Bollinger Convair here saying, we've been harmed by those violations of the antitrust laws that you've committed. They have, so far as the record shows, been perfectly content. We have only the parent here, only the subsidiary here. I revert, Mr. Chief Justice, to the question that you put to me a while ago because I do think that one of the reasons this case has gone on so long and did not come to an end expeditiously as we had anticipated is because of a misunderstanding of what the position was that Tolko took on February 8, 1963 when it announced that it would not defend further on the merits. That has been made to have overtones of contumacy, of scorning the process of the court, and those overtones, in my judgment, are quite unjustified. I think that it is not only proper, it is responsible for a party to avoid factual issues if you can and say, let's simply stake it all on our legal test. We know the facts. We know what we have done. We don't see any way that those facts could possibly be made into a valid antitrust claim. We don't see any way they could possibly prove damages. Why should we go ahead and spend years while people use all the wonderful engines of discovery that the federal rules provide so that we can accumulate thousands of pages of facts when ultimately the court is going to have to decide a straight legal issue? That was the position we took then. We think that would have led to an expeditious termination of the controversy except for one very unfortunate thing, and that is the failure of the district court and then of the court of appeals to give a proper reading to what effect the default has. Those courts took the view that by inviting default, as we certainly did, we had admitted the illegality of what we had done and we had admitted that our illegal acts caused harm. Well, they treated it as though it were a negligence case in which the defendant stipulated negligence and just went to trial on damages. Isn't that about right? A close analogy? I think that that is what they did, and I think that that was giving it too much effect. We waived any right to dispute the facts, but we think that the cases here as written over and over in your books that even after default, a party still retains the right to challenge whether what he has done is a legal wrong, which is the analogy I put in the brief, that a defendant in a criminal case who pleads guilty may still appeal on the ground that the indictment did not state a crime, the law was unconstitutional. We think that the legal questions were still open, and the example of the Section 7 claim in the complaint is the best illustration of that. The complaint says that we acquired the shares of their stock, that we did this to their great damage, and it specifically states a violation of Section 7 of the Clayton Act. But everybody has agreed that there was no Section 7 violation because, as a matter of law, we can't be held to a violated Section 7 when the CAB has said we could acquire the stock. This, at least, is the irreducible minimum that CAB approval allows us. What was it that you said, that your client said, that renders the analogy of conceding negligence and just trying damages, renders that inapposite here? I'm sorry, I don't get the thrust of the question. Perhaps I should do it more directly. Why isn't this, then? What do you rely on to say that this is not like a case of conceding negligence and just going to trial, going to either the trier on the damage issue? It would be like that only if we were in a jurisdiction in which negligence is no longer a sufficient basis for recovery. So that we might admit the fact of negligence by a default but say, well, to hear for this kind of action you have to prove willful and wrong an injury or something of that sort. Of course, Chief Justice Example, it's stated that negligence was conceded. Yeah. Your point is here you've never conceded the violation of the antitrust. That's right. You've never conceded liability, is your point. We have never conceded liability. You've conceded all the facts, but you say they don't add up to antitrust liability. That is precisely what we're saying, Justice Brennan. That as a matter of law, the facts that their complaint alleges and that the damage hearing established do not add up to an antitrust violation. With the court's permission, I would like to reserve my remaining time for a buck. Very well. Mr. Wright, Mr. Tenney. Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the court. I am here on behalf of Transworld Airlines, TWA, and 35,000 public stockholders. According to defendants, they have no claim to economic independence and no right to relief under the antitrust laws. This case is almost 12 years old now. The judgment below is a result of unanimity below. The special master, who was Herbert Brownell, the district judge, Charles Metzner, and two panels of the Court of Appeals have been in full agreement. Like my opponent, I am going to leave the facts and the history of proceedings to the statement in our brief, which is very detailed and which is documented to the record and which is, as to both the facts and the history of the proceedings, pretty much the same as the courts below saw them. I will also leave to our briefs the four questions that are presented by our cross-petition in number 830. The questions in the cross-petition are pretty straightforward questions of policy and statutory interpretation. And of course, we hope that the Court will agree with us on them, but I don't think they need any special explanation. In 827, the first two questions that this Court granted certiorari on had as their subject the conduct of a pretrial discovery during the first two years of this 12-year-old litigation and the entry of the default judgment when the defendants, expressly refusing to obey court orders, refused to proceed with either pretrial or trial. In the petition and in their initial brief, the defendants claimed that this conduct of the pretrial proceedings, in these ways, they were denied due process of law, a Fifth Amendment point. We haven't heard anything about that in the reply brief or in the oral argument today. The reply brief says that this is all procedural underbrush. But there is one point I would like to make about it. The defendants have had their day in court, their full day in court on these points. On March 8th of 1965, the Court, this Court, entered an order dismissing certiorari in number 501 of that term. That order disposed, finally, of the appeal that Hughes Tool Company had taken from the dismissal with prejudice of its counterclaims, counterclaims against TWA as well as a number of other additional defendants. That was a default judgment entered in favor of TWA as well as these counterclaim defendants when the Tool Company formally and expressly refused in open court to proceed with pretrial or trial of the factual issues of the entire litigation. The same refusals that are before you on those questions today. In 501, this appeal presented the questions of whether the pretrial proceedings had been properly handled by the district court, whether the discovery orders complained of were proper, whether the entry of a default judgment was justified when the defendants refused to obey those orders and announced that they would not proceed further. Those are the first two questions before the court today. The excuse for raising them again is that the scope of the interlocutory appeal, 443 of that term, was restricted to jurisdictional questions. But a restriction on the permissive interlocutory appeal is really beside the point. Even if there had been no interlocutory appeal at all, if the permission had been refused to take that appeal, 501 would have reached the discovery orders the defendant's refusal to proceed and the entry under Rule 37 of a default judgment because of those events. And as far as those questions are concerned, this court's order in number 501 operated as a final order. We think that as a matter of judicial finality, the principles of this court has laid down, there's no reason to look at those questions at any subsequent stage of the litigation. And the Court of Appeals, of course, disagreed with us on this. They looked again, they reviewed the record again, they came out with a second unanimous decision. That there was no error in the pretrial proceedings, the discovery orders were proper, and that, and I'll quote the 1971 opinion on this, were less at stake in this litigation, the propriety of the default judgment would not have deserved the full discussion we have afforded. The entry of the default judgment was inescapable and virtually invited by Tullco. I don't believe any of the defendant's procedural arguments in their brief, need any further comment besides, of course, what we have in our brief. Now, as I see it, the defendants are presenting two questions of substantive law, I suppose. I only see two. They're at a trust defense and they're CAB defense. Those are the same questions that they raised on the prior interlocutory appeal. They are still presented only on the pleadings, or at least that's the way they should be presented. There has still been no trial on the merits, and it is still true, now as it was in 1965, that the reason there hasn't been any trial is because defendants decided a responsible business decision to prevent one in 1963. But as I hear them today, they are still denying matters alleged in the complaint. They are still arguing their factual view of these matters that were at issue. The conduit theory of the ordering of jets, that this was solely for TWA. They are denying that they tried to establish themselves as a dominant factor in the supply of aircraft to airlines, that they seized the TWA market, imposed boycotts, and prevented TWA from acquiring sufficient aircraft and arranging financing so that they could do this, so that the diversions of aircraft from TWA to its competitors had as a very specific purpose the establishment of defendants as a factor, a competitive factor, in the business of supplying aircraft to airlines. Mr. Tenney? Yes, sir. If this court should hold that a subsidiary does not have any post-acquisition antitrust claim available to it under the law against a parent, would you think that was something that these petitioners couldn't raise because of the default? No, Your Honor. I believe that the default does not preclude them from raising complete legal defenses that are presented by the pleadings. They would not be barred from raising that point. I frankly can't conceive of this court coming to that conclusion in the light of the history of its decisions. Do you know of any cases from this court that have authorized that sort of a suit where the subsidiary is a plaintiff and the parent is a defendant? Well, Your Honor, every derivative suit that involves the antitrust laws in which the subsidiary sues its parent clearly involves this matter. There have been several of them that the court has denied certiorari on. But they're asserting the claim of the parent, aren't they? They aren't asserting a claim against the parent. They're purporting to assert the claim of the parent. No, there aren't derivative suits by stockholders of a minority-owned subsidiary against the parent. Is your opponent correct in saying that these suits regard with respect to the acquisition? No, Your Honor, he's not. There are several cases in which that is not the case. No, you've got those in your brain. I believe so, sir. Moreover, the question, basically, is whether there is a violation of the antitrust laws. Now, if the subsidiary can't sue because there has been no violation of the antitrust laws, nobody can sue. The government can't sue for an injunction. So, therefore, cases like the Timken Roller-Bearing case, the Permalife Mufflers case, Fortner against U.S. Steel, third, if there is no antitrust violation, if that is the reason why the subsidiary can't sue, then the entire scope of the antitrust laws has been gravely diminished. What if the reason the subsidiary can't sue is that it fails to meet the damages requirement of the triple damages section, injured by reason of and so forth? If any plaintiff fails to meet the damages requirement that he is injured by reason of violation of the antitrust law, he's out of court. That wouldn't preclude a government suit out of the same circumstance. No, it would not. But that is not my opponent's argument here. My opponent's argument is the subsidiary can't sue. He's disqualified just because it's the subsidiary. But you don't contend then that the default admitted any violation of the antitrust law? The default... As such? As such? No, Your Honor. It did not. It admitted all of the conduct. It admitted the purposes. The anti-competitive... It admits the historical facts. The historical facts and the anti-competitive purposes, the intent to monopolize... The historical facts, you're saying... Yes, sir. Those are facts. Those are facts. They are admitted. It also happens to be the case, of course, that there is a concession here that the complaint states the cause of action under the antitrust laws. That's illegal. But that has been conceded, actually, in the briefs. The default doesn't concede a violation of the antitrust law? The default does not. As a matter of law, the allegations are sufficient to establish. So whether the facts that have led to a violation of the antitrust laws is a question of law that... That is a question of law. ...on which your to your right to damages the merits. Yes, it does, Your Honor. If we had not alleged a violation of the antitrust laws in this complaint... You mean if you have not alleged facts? If we have not alleged the facts... ...which add up to a violation of the antitrust laws, then you're out of court. Exactly, Your Honor. That has been the case right along. Or if those... Even if there's a violation, if there isn't causation. Well, causation is a... Causation is a peculiar word, Your Honor, in this context. It's called proximate cause in the final question as it was presented to this court in the petition for certiorari. But that's... Really, that's an argument of desperation. This... What happened to TWA here wasn't some accidental explosion like the Paulsgraf case. Everything that was done to TWA was done deliberately. Well, yeah, but everything that... Every kind of damage imaginable that happened to TWA during these years can't be charged to... to... to use... to use... to go... Of course not, Your Honor. Resulted from the antitrust law. Of course not, Your Honor. Only damages that are traceable precisely as we have traced every element of damages that has been... that is the basis of our damage award to the conduct that is alleged in the complaint as having been done by the defendants pursuant to their illegal conspiracy and restraint of trade. For example, six Boeing jets, six of the first jets that went into service in this country, were diverted by the defendants from TWA to TWA's principal transatlantic competitor, Pan America. Now, that diversion is admitted. That it was pursuant to the conspiracy and restraint of trade in order to establish themselves in the market, that's admitted. Our damages... That really isn't admitted, is it? Yes, it is, sir. In restraint of trade? To a conspiracy in restraint of trade. Well, that's illegal. I don't think so, sir. Isn't that just mismanagement? In restraint of trade? I don't see that this mismanagement when the purpose is to establish a... to establish the defendants through use of the TWA market as a dominant factor in the supply of aircraft to airlines. It's mismanagement also. There's mismanagement involved in it. Certainly, TWA got badly hurt by its manager, but it got badly hurt for purposes that its manager had on the outside. And those purposes were anti-competitive. There's a lot of... There's a great deal of mismanagement involved in many antitrust cases. But that doesn't make them any less antitrust cases. Well, do you have a mismanagement case which involves antitrust, which is caught, as said, violent antitrust where there was a subsidiary and a parent corporation involved? I'm not sure that I can think of one where mismanagement has been expressly referred to. Well, you said mismanagement and antitrust, they're always tied up together. I just want to... No, sir. I don't mean that they're always... I want to get one closer in on this case. No, sir. I don't mean that they're always tied up together, but I mean that many violations of various kinds of law are also violations of the antitrust laws, and mismanagement can be one of them. under your question to my brother Rankish, he said you don't have a case that says that the subsidiary can recover against the principle on antitrust. I don't have a case that has been decided by this court on that precise point, sir. There are cases in the lower courts, some of them... Is that the point in this case? Well, the defendants have presented this as the point. They've developed a new doctrine. It's new to me under the antitrust laws. They have constructed a doctrine applicable to what they call a parent-subsidiary relationship that puts everything in that relationship outside of the scope of the antitrust laws. They say that as long as the parent controls the subsidiary... The burden's not on them, the burden's on you. You allege the antitrust violations, right? The burden is on me at a trial to establish the violations, Your Honor. There was no trial. And that it stands where the plaintiff is the subsidiary against the parent. That's also your burden.
